title: The Infinite-Dimensional Cayley-Hamilton Analog: Compact Operators on Hilbert Spaces
description: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem (charpoly(A)(A) = 0) has no direct analog in infinite dimensions because there is no finite-degree characteristic polynomial. For compact operators on Hilbert spaces, the analog is the Fredholm alternative and spectral projection decomposition: the spectrum is discrete with eigenvalues converging to 0, and each nonzero spectral value admits a finite-dimensional spectral projection.

overview.historicalContext: Fredholm (1903) studied integral equations and discovered the alternative: either a unique solution exists or the homogeneous equation has nontrivial solutions. Hilbert (1906) proved the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators. Riesz (1918) extended this to general compact operators with his theory of compact operators on Banach spaces. Schauder (1930) further developed the Riesz-Schauder theory. The modern formulation uses continuous linear maps on Hilbert spaces.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question**: What is the analog of Cayley-Hamilton reduction for infinite-dimensional operators (compact operators on Hilbert spaces)?

**Answer**: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem (charpoly(A)(A) = 0) generalizes to three key results for compact operators: (1) the spectrum is discrete with eigenvalues converging to 0, (2) the Fredholm alternative holds at each nonzero spectral value, and (3) spectral projections provide the decomposition analogous to polynomial reduction.
overview.text: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem has no direct analog in infinite dimensions because there is no finite-degree characteristic polynomial. For compact operators on Hilbert spaces, the analog is the Fredholm alternative and spectral projection decomposition: the spectrum is discrete with eigenvalues converging to 0, and each nonzero spectral value admits a finite-dimensional spectral projection.
overview.proofStrategy: We define compact operators as bounded operators mapping the closed unit ball to a relatively compact set, then establish algebraic closure properties (zero, scalar, composition). We axiomatize the three deep theorems (Riesz-Schauder, Fredholm alternative, spectral decomposition) and prove structural consequences. The analogy theorem packages the three infinite-dimensional analogs of the finite-dimensional Cayley-Hamilton features.
keyInsights: Compact operators are 'close to finite-dimensional': they are norm-limits of finite-rank operators, inheriting finite-like spectral theory
The Fredholm alternative is the precise analog of Cayley-Hamilton: at each nonzero lambda, (lambda I - T) is either invertible or has nontrivial kernel, with no continuous spectrum
Spectral projections (via Riesz contour integrals) replace polynomial reduction: instead of reducing mod charpoly, decompose the operator into spectral components
Each nonzero eigenvalue of a compact operator has finite multiplicity (finite-dimensional eigenspace), exactly paralleling the finite degree of the characteristic polynomial
The spectrum of a compact operator is at most countable with 0 as the only possible accumulation point, giving a 'discrete characteristic polynomial'
prerequisites: Inner product spaces and Hilbert space completeness
Bounded (continuous) linear operators and operator norm
Topological compactness and the Heine-Borel property
Eigenvalues and eigenspaces for linear operators

sections.title: Compact Operators: Definition and Algebraic Properties
sections.summary: Defines IsCompactOp as a predicate on ContinuousLinearMap. Proves closure properties: zero is compact, scalar multiples are compact, left-composition with bounded is compact.
sections.mathContext: A bounded operator $T: H \to H$ is **compact** if $\overline{T(\overline{B_1(0)})}$ is compact. Compact operators form a two-sided ideal in $\mathcal{B}(H)$: closed under sum, scalar multiplication, and composition with bounded operators.

sections.title: Spectral Properties: Discrete Spectrum and Finite Multiplicity
sections.summary: Defines eigenvalues and eigenspaces. Proves eigenspace is a subspace. Axiomatizes the Riesz-Schauder theorem (discrete spectrum with eigenvalues converging to 0). States finite multiplicity for nonzero eigenvalues.
sections.mathContext: **Riesz-Schauder theorem**: For compact $T$, $\sigma(T) \setminus \{0\}$ is at most countable with 0 as the only accumulation point. Each $\lambda \neq 0$ in $\sigma(T)$ is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional eigenspace. This parallels the finite-dimensional case where $\text{deg}(\text{charpoly}) = n$ bounds the multiplicity.

sections.title: The Fredholm Alternative: The Infinite-Dimensional Cayley-Hamilton
sections.summary: Axiomatizes the Fredholm alternative: for compact T and nonzero lambda, either (lambda I - T) is invertible or lambda is an eigenvalue. Proves the corollary: no continuous spectrum at nonzero values.
sections.mathContext: **Fredholm alternative** (1903): For compact $T$ and $\lambda \neq 0$: either $\lambda I - T$ is bijective (resolvent point) or $\ker(\lambda I - T) \neq 0$ (eigenvalue). No third case. This is the precise analog of Cayley-Hamilton: the characteristic polynomial's roots are exactly the eigenvalues, and all other scalars give invertible $(\lambda I - A)$.

sections.title: Spectral Projection Decomposition
sections.summary: Defines SpectralProjection structure (idempotent, commutes with T). Axiomatizes existence of spectral projections at each eigenvalue. This replaces polynomial reduction in finite dimensions.
sections.mathContext: The **Riesz spectral projection** for isolated eigenvalue $\lambda$ of compact $T$: $P_\lambda = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_\gamma (\mu I - T)^{-1} d\mu$ where $\gamma$ encircles $\lambda$ only. Properties: $P_\lambda^2 = P_\lambda$, $P_\lambda T = T P_\lambda$, $\text{range}(P_\lambda)$ is the generalized eigenspace. This replaces polynomial reduction: instead of $f(A) \equiv f \mod \text{charpoly}(A)$, we have $f(T) P_\lambda$ depending only on $f$ near $\lambda$.

sections.title: The Precise Analogy: Finite vs Infinite Dimensions
sections.summary: Defines HasAnnihilatingPoly and HasFiniteDimSpectralSubspaces. Proves the cayley_hamilton_analogy theorem packaging all three infinite-dimensional analogs: Fredholm alternative, discrete spectrum, and spectral projections.
sections.mathContext: The three pillars of the analogy: (1) Cayley-Hamilton ($p(A) = 0$) $\leftrightarrow$ Fredholm alternative (resolvent/eigenvalue dichotomy), (2) finite-degree charpoly $\leftrightarrow$ eigenvalues converging to 0, (3) polynomial reduction $\leftrightarrow$ spectral projection decomposition. Compact operators bridge finite and infinite dimensions because they are norm-limits of finite-rank operators.

conclusion.summary: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem for finite-dimensional matrices generalizes to compact operators on Hilbert spaces via three key results: the Riesz-Schauder theorem (discrete spectrum), the Fredholm alternative (invertible-or-eigenvalue dichotomy), and spectral projection decomposition (Riesz projections). Compact operators are the natural infinite-dimensional setting because they are 'close to finite-dimensional' as norm-limits of finite-rank operators.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's open question: the computational efficiency of Cayley-Hamilton reduction for sparse matrices has an infinite-dimensional analog when the operator is compact. The spectral projection decomposition decomposes the operator into finite-dimensional pieces (one per eigenvalue), each of which can be analyzed using finite-dimensional techniques.
openQuestions: Can the spectral decomposition be made computationally efficient for specific classes of compact operators (e.g., integral operators with smooth kernels)?
What is the analog for non-compact operators with essential spectrum?
Can Fredholm determinants provide a true infinite-dimensional 'characteristic polynomial'?
